lab_title: VSEPR: Predicting Molecular Geometry from Lewis Structures
top_level_objectives: Use VSEPR electron-domain ideas to predict molecular geometry for common covalent molecules
Identify electron-domain geometry from the number of bonding regions and lone pairs on the central atom
Determine how lone pairs modify idealized bond angles and molecular shape
Compare AR-predicted geometries with real molecules (water, ammonia, methane, PF5, SF6, XeF4) and explain discrepancies due to lone-pair repulsion and angular space demands

scenes.scene_name: Orient to VSEPR: From Lewis Structure to Electron Domains
scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the AR workflow and the core VSEPR concept: electron pairs arrange to minimize repulsion; define electron domains as bonding regions and lone pairs.
key_visuals: A central atom with highlighted electron domains (bonding regions vs lone pairs) derived from an example Lewis structure
A schematic “repulsion map” showing domains spreading apart in 3D
A legend labeling electron domains and molecular shape placeholders
student_actions: Select/confirm which electron domains are present (bonding pairs and lone pairs) on the central atom.
Count electron domains and record the implied electron-domain geometry choice.
State the initial hypothesis for the molecular shape that will result once lone pairs are included.

scenes.scene_name: Electron-Domain Geometries I: Linear, Trigonal Planar, Tetrahedral
scenes.brief_purpose: Build intuition for the first three VSEPR electron-domain geometries and how zero vs nonzero lone pairs produce the common molecular shapes.
key_visuals: AR 3D models for linear (2 domains), trigonal planar (3 domains), and tetrahedral (4 domains) with ideal bond angles displayed
Interactive toggles showing lone pairs as extra repelling domains
Real-time geometry “settling” from flexible starting positions into idealized arrangements
student_actions: For each model, drag domains into place or confirm they settle into the correct electron-domain geometry.
Turn lone pairs on/off and predict how the molecular shape changes (e.g., bent from tetrahedral with lone pairs).
Measure and note bond angles against the ideal values before applying lone-pair corrections.

scenes.scene_name: Electron-Domain Geometries II: Trigonal Bipyramidal and Octahedral
scenes.brief_purpose: Teach the special positioning rules in trigonal bipyramidal (axial vs equatorial) and octahedral arrangements, then show how lone pairs alter the final molecular geometry.
key_visuals: AR representation of trigonal bipyramidal with axial/equatorial axes labeled and 90°/120° references
A second set for octahedral with six domain positions and labeled angles
A visualization of lone pairs taking positions that maximize separation (e.g., equatorial preference)
student_actions: For PF5/SF4-like electron-domain counts, choose where lone pairs should locate to minimize repulsion.
Predict the resulting molecular geometries (trigonal pyramidal/bent-like from trigonal bipyramidal; square planar/square pyramidal from octahedral cases).
Verify by letting the geometry settle and checking whether the predicted axial/equatorial placement matches.

scenes.scene_name: Bond Angles and Lone-Pair Effects: Why Real Angles Deviate
scenes.brief_purpose: Explain quantitatively/qualitatively that lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, causing smaller bond angles than ideal.
key_visuals: Overlay comparing ideal geometry angles to “observed” angles with adjustable lone-pair count
A comparative view: water vs ammonia vs methane angle change (e.g., ~104.5° vs 109.5°)
A repulsion strength indicator showing lone pairs as stronger repulsors than bonding pairs
student_actions: Choose a molecule (e.g., water, ammonia, methane) and predict the direction of bond-angle deviation from the ideal angle.
Adjust the number/type of electron domains and observe how angles compress as lone pairs increase.
Write a short explanation for the deviation using the concept of angular space demand.

scenes.scene_name: Match Predictions to Real Molecules: Water, Ammonia, Methane, PF5, SF6, XeF4
scenes.brief_purpose: Have students apply the complete VSEPR workflow to multiple real molecules and compare AR predictions to known structures.
key_visuals: A gallery of molecule cards with Lewis-structure prompts for: H2O, NH3, CH4, PF5, SF6, XeF4
For each molecule: an AR predicted 3D model with electron domains and final molecular geometry highlighted
A “prediction vs structure” toggle showing how well the AR model matches reference observations
student_actions: For each molecule, count electron domains and determine the electron-domain geometry, then the molecular shape.
Activate the “compare to reference” view and judge agreement (match/partial match) visually.
Record any deviations and attribute them to lone-pair effects (noting which molecules have lone pairs).

scenes.scene_name: Consolidation: From Geometry to General Rules
scenes.brief_purpose: Synthesize VSEPR rules into a concise checklist that students can reuse on new Lewis structures.
key_visuals: A summary flowchart mapping number of electron domains → electron-domain geometry → molecular shape options
A bond-angle correction note: lone pairs < bonding pairs in angular space impact (trend arrows)
A final AR “challenge prompt” with an unseen central-atom Lewis structure (no full solution shown)
student_actions: Use the flowchart to predict geometry for the challenge molecule by applying the same steps (count domains → place lone pairs → determine molecular shape).
Check the AR settlement and compare with the predicted shape.
Submit a brief justification: state the electron-domain geometry and how lone pairs change bond angles or shape.
